title: Parameterized Inapproximability Hypothesis from \(\mathrm{FPT} \ne  \mathrm{W}[1]\)
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Assuming \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\), is there an absolute constant \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) such that no deterministic fixed-parameter algorithm can distinguish a satisfiable binary constraint satisfaction instance on k variables from an instance in which every assignment violates at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of the constraints, with k as the parameter?
context:
Exact unsatisfiability only says every assignment fails somewhere. PIH asks for a constant fraction of failures on every assignment. If an instance has many constraints, the existence of just one unavoidable violation need not give any fixed gap.

The alphabet is allowed to grow with the input. Exhaustive search takes \(n^{k}\) time, whose exponent depends on k; that is not fixed-parameter tractable. A running time such as \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) would qualify despite its very large dependence on k.

Baby PIH distinguishes satisfiable instances from instances for which even a constant-size list of values at each variable cannot satisfy every constraint. This is a different guarantee from saying that every ordinary assignment violates a constant fraction of constraints.

The Guruswami–Lin–Ren–Sun–Wu theorem derives PIH from the Exponential Time Hypothesis. ETH imposes a quantitative subexponential-time obstruction for 3SAT and is a stronger assumption than the parameterized separation sought here. The February 2026 survey still separates these targets.
why: Would supply a parameterized analogue of the PCP theorem from the standard exact-hardness assumption, giving a common basis for constant-gap inapproximability across many parameterized optimization problems.
status_note: Source definitions, the ETH theorem and the February 2026 survey checked with later-result searches through 12 September 2026. No proof under only \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) was located.

progress.text: Baby PIH is established under \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\); the full PIH implication is left open.
The journal version of PIH under ETH records the stronger-assumption theorem, whose preprint already appeared in 2023.
The survey explicitly retains the distinction between PIH under ETH and PIH under \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\).

The question asks whether it also rules out distinguishing satisfiable binary constraint systems from systems that force a constant fraction of violations.
The parameter is the number of variables, while the alphabet may grow with the input.
PIH is already known under the stronger ETH assumption, and Baby PIH is known under \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\).

definitions: A binary constraint satisfaction instance has k variables, a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of size n, and explicitly given binary relations specifying the allowed pairs for constrained variable pairs. Its finite input length includes these relation tables. An assignment chooses one alphabet value for each variable; \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\) is the maximum fraction of its constraints satisfied by an assignment. The promise is \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )=1\) or \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\le 1- \varepsilon\); no answer is prescribed for intermediate values. For an instance of encoded size L, fixed-parameter tractable means time \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) for some computable f and constant C independent of k and L. In the standard representation with one binary relation per constrained pair, this is equivalent to \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\) after absorbing polynomial k-factors into f. Here \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) is the standard deterministic hypothesis, equivalently that deciding whether a finite graph has a k-clique has no \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) algorithm. PIH asserts the existence of one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) for which the promised approximation task has no such algorithm, irrespective of the computable function f or constant exponent C. The question is the implication from exact parameterized hardness to that constant-gap hardness, not an unconditional assertion of \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\).
answer_criterion: Establish the stated implication using only \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) as the complexity assumption, with a constant gap independent of k and n, or refute that implication. A result assuming ETH or Gap-ETH, a gap shrinking with k, or hardness for a list-assignment variant does not settle this target.
